Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A plump black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch, with four red, orange, and gold leaves, against a soft, misty sunset forest.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

11 stepsCanvas: 14 x 11 inFocal point: The chickadee's head and black bib, at about 48% across and 20% down in the frame. Light: The low sun, upper right of the bird at 66% across and 15% down in the frame. Lit edges face up and to the right.How this lesson was made

Tubes

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: the glow and hazeFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #6 round: the sunRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #10 flat: pulling the trunksFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat or 1/2 inch flat: tapping foliageOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #8 round: outlining the branchesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: filling the thick partFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #4 round: the twigsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #2 round: the stemsRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the white feather edgesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • A 14 x 11 in canvas, landscape (hang it that way). Positions in the steps are percentages across and down: each 10% is 1.4 in across and 1.1 in down.
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

Your paints

Every paint in the lesson. You don't have to mix them all at the start: each step lists the paints it uses with their recipes, so you can mix a little as you go before it dries. Parts are by volume.

The steps

STEP 1 OF 11

Paint the misty sunset glow

  1. The light comes from the low sun, upper right of the bird (69% across, 15% down). Keep every highlight on that side.
  2. 1 inch flat, creamy Sunset gold: X-stroke a glow around the sun spot, 50 to 90% across, top edge to 35% down.
  3. Blend Glow peach outward from the gold and down the middle to about 65% down, in soft cloudy patches, not clean bands.
  4. Misty lavender down the left side, right edge, and bottom; Haze blue low on the left and in faint upright smudges along the bottom. Blend joins wet.
  5. While the gold is wet, dab a 1/2 inch Sun cream sun at 69% across, 15% down. Let it dry.
Paints for this step5 paints, 5 new
  • Sunset gold new3 parts white, 2 parts orange, 1 part flesh tint
  • Glow peach new3 parts flesh tint, 1 part orange, a touch of light magenta
  • Misty lavender new3 parts flesh tint, 1 part ultramarine
  • Haze blue new1 part ultramarine, 1 part flesh tint, 1 part white, a touch of orange
  • Sun cream new6 parts white, 1 part orange, a touch of yellow deep

Colors dry a little darker: test each mix on the palette edge before the big areas.

Brushes

1 inch flat#6 round

Strokes

X stroke. Criss-cross the flat in overlapping X shapes so neighboring colors melt together with soft texture.

Wet-on-wet blend. Brush lightly back and forth over each join while both colors are wet.

Watch out: Don't leave white where the bird and branch will go: cover the whole canvas, edge to edge.

Watch out: Work fast; stop blending as soon as the paint drags, or it turns muddy.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How this picture was made Render · 1 try · $0.019

Why this step, now: Everything sits on the glow, so it goes first and runs straight under the bird and branch so the blend never breaks.

Why this tool: Render from the finish with later parts left off: no composite tool exists yet (#8), and hiding the bird, branches, and foliage means inventing the haze behind them, which a throwaway inpaint can't do.

No diagram: A blended background; the step picture shows where each color sits.

STEP 2 OF 11

Add the misty far trunks

  1. With the #10 flat nearly dry, pull Trunk gray straight down from the top edge to the bottom edge for a slim trunk at 77 to 81% across.
  2. Pull a wider trunk the same way at 85 to 92% across, splitting it in two near the top.
  3. Add a short faint trunk at 37 to 42% across, from 62% down to the bottom edge.
  4. Soften each trunk's edges with Misty lavender, and haze over the glow beside the right trunks (70 to 80% across, 30 to 60% down). Let it dry.

Try a dry-brush stroke on scrap paper first.

#10 flat

Strokes

Dry brushing. Wipe the flat nearly clean, then pull down with light pressure so the haze shows through the trunk.

Watch out: Dark, crisp trunks look close. Keep them pale and soft-edged.

STEP 3 OF 11

Dab the rust foliage

  1. Load the corner of a stiff flat with creamy Rust orange and tap loose clusters, 1/4 to 3/4 inch each.
  2. Cluster them thickest around the right trunks and down the left side, and fewer and softer inside the gold glow.
  3. Leave lavender haze showing between the clusters. Let it dry.

Brushes

old stiff flat or 1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Dabbing. Tap the brush corner straight down with light pressure, turning it a little each tap so the marks vary.

Watch out: Even rows of dots look like polka dots. Tap in loose groups of three to six.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 11

Dab the peach foliage

  1. Wipe the brush, then tap creamy Foliage peach on the top, sun-facing half of each rust cluster.
  2. Leave the rust showing on the lower half of every cluster, and the haze between them.
  3. Tap a few new peach clusters into the open haze, as the picture shows, and a few soft Sunset gold taps near the sun. Let it dry.

STEP 5 OF 11

Block in the branches

  1. Let the background dry. With the #8 round and creamy Bark dark, outline the big branch as the diagram shows: in at the bottom-left corner, peaking at 50% across, 58% down, out the right edge at 87% down.
  2. Make it about 2 inches thick at the bottom left, tapering to 1/4 inch past the middle. Fill the thick part with the 1/2 inch flat.
  3. Pull the thin branch from the big one at 9% across, 68% down, straight up to the top edge at 4% across, with a twig to 15% across, 10% down.
  4. With the #4 round, press and lift three twigs off the right half, as in the diagram. Let it dry.
Paints for this step1 paint, 1 new
  • Bark dark new1 part burnt umber, a touch of purple red

Brushes

#8 round1/2 inch flat#4 round

Strokes

Thick-to-thin. Press the belly of the brush down at the thick end and lift slowly as you pull, so the line tapers.

Press and lift. Touch down, pull a short stroke, and lift off to a point for each twig.

Watch out: An even-width branch looks like a pipe. Press hard near the trunk and lift as you go.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 11

Light the bark

  1. With the #8 round and creamy Bark mid, stroke along the top half of both branches, following the curve.
  2. Leave a strip of Bark dark showing along every underside, with a few Haze blue touches under the thick part.
  3. Add a few short Bark light patches on top of the thick part, 12 to 34% across, and touch Bark mid along the twigs' tops. Let it dry.

STEP 7 OF 11

Paint the four leaves

  1. Build each leaf as in the diagram: a center line, then each half outlined with the #8 round and filled with the 1/2 inch flat, to a point. Notch the edges a little.
  2. Leaf gold at the top, 15 to 32% across, from the top edge to 18% down. Leaf red below it, 10 to 23% across, 14 to 37% down, tip down.
  3. Pull a thin Leaf red stem down from the big branch at 65% across, 67% down.
  4. Hang a Leaf orange leaf from it, gold on its right half (49 to 65% across, 71 to 93% down), and a Leaf red leaf at 65 to 79% across, 79% down to the bottom edge.
  5. Blend Leaf orange into one half of each red leaf, as the picture shows. Let it dry.

STEP 8 OF 11

Block in the bird's body

  1. The bird goes on dry paint. With the 1/2 inch flat and creamy Flank buff, paint an egg-shaped body, 37 to 60% across and 26 to 56% down (about 3 by 3 1/4 inches).
  2. Wet-blend Breast cream down its right, sun-facing side.
  3. With the #8 round, lay a Wing gray wing along the body's left side and a long tail to 13% across, 61% down, as in the diagram.
  4. Leave the head area as background for now. Let it dry.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat#8 round

Strokes

Curved strokes that follow a form. Stroke around the oval, curving with the body, so it looks round.

Building from pieces. Body oval first, then the wing over its left side, then the tail.

Watch out: A flat, pancake body: keep the oval full and round.

Watch out: This is the ugly stage, when a painting often looks wrong. That's normal; keep going.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 9 OF 11

Paint the head

  1. With the #8 round and Cap black, paint a rounded cap over the head, 38 to 58% across, top at 11% down, as in the diagram.
  2. With Cheek white, paint the cheek band right across the head below the cap, 38 to 55% across, 21 to 29% down.
  3. With Cap black, add the bib below the band on the right, 47 to 58% across, down to 32% down, over the top of the breast. Two coats if it looks gray. Let it dry.

STEP 10 OF 11

Shade the feathers

  1. With the #4 round and Feather dark, paint three or four stripes along the wing, down-left. Let them dry.
  2. With the liner, edge each stripe with a thin Cheek white line, and pull a few Feather dark and Cheek white lines along the tail.
  3. Flick short fur strokes around the body's curve: Flank buff underneath and on the left, Breast cream on the right side facing the sun.
  4. Soften the cheek's lower edge with short Cheek white flicks. Let it dry.

Why this step, now: Eye, beak, feet, and brightest highlights last, over dry paint.

Why this tool: Render from the finish with later parts left off: no composite tool exists yet (#8), and hiding the bird, branches, and foliage means inventing the haze behind them, which a throwaway inpaint can't do.

No diagram: Small marks placed by grid numbers.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A chickadee on an autumn branch against a misty sunset forest

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No screen, page, or border around it.

Fitted to your canvas

Canvas: 14 x 11 in, landscape (an 11x14 hung sideways)

Done: crop

Left out: about 11% off the top (the top of the gold leaf and some glow) and 11% off the bottom (the tip of the lower red leaf and haze)

Why: The picture is square; fit-canvas picked landscape and a crop, which keeps the whole bird, the branch, and all four leaves.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes, dozens of thorny nubs and buds along every twig. Textures of hundreds of items: yes, feather-by-feather fur and a thick bark patchwork. Detail inside big shapes: yes, veined, jagged leaves and textured misty trees. Parts: about 9, over the budget of 8.

Changed: Dropped the twig nubs and most tiny twigs; bark became a smooth branch with a dark underside and a few lighter strokes; misty trees became a few soft trunks with loose foliage dabs; the bird's fur became smooth blended paint and the wing three or four stripes; leaves became smooth with one vein.

Why: With those gone the picture is about 7 parts, each one a shape or one repeated mark.

A soft, glowing autumn picture: the chickadee is the whole point, so its black cap, white cheek, and black bib must read crisply against a hazy, warm background. The hard parts are the bird's shape and markings, and keeping the background misty instead of busy.

Subject: A plump black-capped chickadee perched on a curved autumn branch, with four red, orange, and gold leaves, against a soft, misty sunset forest.
Focal point: The chickadee's head and black bib, at about 48% across and 20% down in the frame.
Light: The low sun, upper right of the bird at 66% across and 15% down in the frame. Lit edges face up and to the right.

What it saw, back to front

  1. misty sunset glow and sun
  2. far trunks
  3. foliage dabs (rust, then peach)
  4. branches
  5. bark light
  6. leaves
  7. bird body, wing, tail
  8. bird head
  9. feathers
  10. eye, beak, feet, highlights
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

The owner named acrylic-paint-along-beginner.

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

The owner named paint-along, and it fits: a soft background first, the branch on top, then the bird built from simple shapes, the way YouTube bird tutorials go.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

Not chosen: the owner named the technique. Block-in's toned ground and sketch would also fight the soft, wet-blended glow.

How the paint recipes were worked out20 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order11 steps

Back to front: the glow and haze over the whole canvas, the far trunks, two passes of misty foliage (dark, then light), the branches (dark, then lit bark), the leaves on the branch, then the bird body, head, and feathers, and the small details last.

  1. 1. Paint the misty sunset glow

    Everything sits on the glow, so it goes first and runs straight under the bird and branch so the blend never breaks.

  2. 2. Add the misty far trunks

    Farthest solid things; pale and soft so they stay in the haze.

  3. 3. Dab the rust foliage

    The foliage is a dense dab texture, so it's split into passes; the darker rust goes first.

  4. 4. Dab the peach foliage

    Second pass: peach on the sun-facing half of each cluster, so the foliage builds up instead of arriving finished.

  5. 5. Block in the branches

    The branch is the nearest big shape behind the bird; a flat dark base first.

  6. 6. Light the bark

    Mid and light on top of the dark base give the branch three values and its roundness.

  7. 7. Paint the four leaves

    The leaves hang from the branches, so they go on after them and before the bird, which is the front-most thing.

  8. 8. Block in the bird's body

    The subject gets a teacher's steps: the body shapes first.

  9. 9. Paint the head

    The markings are what makes it a chickadee, so they get their own step on a dry body.

  10. 10. Shade the feathers

    Shading and texture after the base shapes, before the tiny details.

  11. 11. Add the eye, beak, feet, and highlights

    Eye, beak, feet, and brightest highlights last, over dry paint.

Filters it tried11 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams4 steps, free

The bird, its head markings, the leaves, and the branch arc each needed a picture of how to build them; the background steps are blends and dabs the words cover. Checking the words against the canvas grid corrected two sizes: the body is about 3 by 3 1/4 inches and the branch about 2 inches thick at the bottom left.

  • Step 5: Block in the branches beginner check

    Noticed: A long arcing branch that must taper, with a second branch and twigs joining it; where each starts isn't obvious.

    Pieces: The big arc first, thick end at the corner, then the thin branch up from its join, then the three twigs.

  • Step 7: Paint the four leaves beginner check

    Noticed: Four shaped leaves appear at once.

    Pieces: A center line, then a curved half on each side, the way press-and-lift leaves are taught.

  • Step 8: Block in the bird's body beginner check

    Noticed: An animal appears whole in one step.

    Pieces: An egg-shaped body, a long wing ellipse tilted down-left over its left side, then a tail wedge to the lower left.

  • Step 9: Paint the head beginner check

    Noticed: Three markings in a set order on a small head; the reviewer found the cheek band and bib easy to get wrong.

    Pieces: Cap over the top, a white band below it right across the head, then the bib below on the right.

What the reviewer caught30 notes

A second Claude, with fresh eyes and none of this reasoning, compared each picture with its neighbors and the finish. It gets two rounds of fixes, then stops; anything still off is flagged on its step. A third checked each step's words against a measured map of what the picture changed, asking whether a beginner following them would get there.

  • Finish check The haze between the foliage dabs turned a clear sky blue instead of the beginner version's muted gray-lavender
  • Finish check The background foliage dabs were brighter and more saturated than the soft, hazy peach-orange of the beginner version
  • Finish check The warm glow around the sun was too small; it should spread from behind the bird's head to the upper right
  • Round 1 Step 3: The faint middle trunk at 39-43% across grew to start about 28% down instead of 62%. (redone)
  • Round 1 Step 4: Adds whole new foliage clusters where the rust pass had plain haze (center and upper middle). (redone neighbor foliage-dark: the finish has foliage across the center too, so the rust pass was the one too sparse)
  • Round 1 Step 5: The faint middle trunk reappears from about 22% down instead of 60%. (left: outside the step's regions, so lock-steps put the earlier pixels back (no render))
  • Round 2 Step 3: The gold glow shrank to a small patch around the sun, and the rust dabs didn't line up with the rust under the peach in the next step and the finish. (redone)
  • Round 2 Step 9: The black cap ran straight into the bib with no white between, unlike the next step and the finish. (redone)

  • Text check: missing Step 2: The glow beside the right trunks turns lavender (70-80% across, 30-60% down), more than softening edges. (fixed)

  • Text check: diagram Step 3: Proposed a tap-by-tap cluster diagram. (skipped: one repeated tapping mark; the picture shows the clusters, and the beginner check found no shape to build)
  • Text check: drift Step 4: Rust clusters from the step before move or disappear; the bottom-left one becomes haze. (left)

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • fit-canvas picked landscape for a square picture with --orientation auto; it worked here, but the skill doesn't say how a square picture picks its orientation.
  • The canvas fill render also warmed the colors a little inside the canvas area; the painter never sees the filled bands, so no harm, but the render isn't strictly 'change nothing'.
  • On a misty picture both the beginner version and the first finish pushed the haze toward saturated orange and clear blue; the finish prompt needed an explicit 'keep it misty' line.
  • Mean shift at strength 2 was the right reference for a small bird: Kuwahara at 2 and 3 erased the eye, beak, and feet (adds to the stars note in step 1).
  • Round 2's review contradicted round 1 on where the rust dabs go; comparing with the finish settled it (dabs everywhere the finish has foliage, fewer in the glow), and the plan's looks_like was corrected to match.
  • The research notes don't cover birds or fur; the bird's construction (egg body, wing, tail, then cap, cheek, bib) comes from general drawing practice, not the cited notes.
  • step-pairs reads the canvas/ crops from the last publish, so after a redo and lock-steps it shows stale pictures until publish (or canvas-view) runs again. The skill's order (publish, then step-pairs) hides this, but a redo between them doesn't.
  • The step review found that step-sized leaves (1.5 to 2 inches) can't come from one press-and-lift per half with a #8 round; on an 11x14, shapes over an inch need outline-and-fill with a flat.
